items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘Every day, someone loses a hand or a leg’: the brutal reality of India’s textile recycling industry
items.content_html:
In Panipat, 1m tons of used clothing a year are turned into products for global brands, but dangerous machinery and few safeguards mean life-changing injuries are common

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.

Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.

items.title: [apnews.com] Paraguay president submits resignation as Ueno collapse freezes millions of accounts
items.content_html: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña submitted his resignation on Nov. 5 as the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank froze access to accounts held by nearly 3 million customers. Minutes later, the Chamber of Deputies voted 78-0 to impeach him. Congress had not accepted the resignation by Friday, Nov. 6, leaving Peña formally in office. He said he would appear at the Senate proceedings to defend himself. Vice President Pedro Alliana is next in line if lawmakers accept Peña’s resignation or remove him through impeachment. Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno on Nov. 3 after finding that its solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum. The intervention shut down the bank’s app, cards and transfers. Ueno had about 3 million customers and administered roughly $850 million in public funds, including pension-related money. Lawmakers accuse Peña of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and shielding the bank from scrutiny. He has denied wrongdoing and said the matter should be handled through the courts. Prosecutors ordered three investigations into the bank’s failure, covering oversight, the handling of its collapse and the placement of public funds.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated | Patience Akumu
items.content_html:
I wanted to be a beacon of black feminist love; my friends and family teased me for being a sellout

We had been together 20 years, had two children and had a customary marriage with our village sub-county two years ago without any real plans for a church wedding. So we called our second ceremony a celebration of love and not a wedding. How else would a self-professed African feminist survive being the centre of a colonial and Abrahamic religious ceremony that also manages to reinforce the most male-centred aspects of African culture?

Our invitations came directly from me and my partner Mark, not – as is traditional – from our families, and in the form of a playful gif featuring the song Love Potion from the South African group Mafikizolo, a reminder that this was a wedding on our terms. I thought they screamed “liberated African feminist”. But when my cousin Moses received his, he asked, “So, the patriarchy has won?”

items.title: [firstpost.com] Israeli opposition backs Eisenkot as Arab parties hold balance of power
items.content_html: Israeli opposition leaders are meeting Tuesday to coordinate support for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government after an October 27 election left no bloc with a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp won 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Jewish-led opposition parties won 48. Arab-majority parties won 19, making their support potentially decisive. The opposition’s central dispute is whether to rely on Arab lawmakers. Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, supports cooperation, while Avigdor Lieberman of Yisrael Beiteinu opposes an Arab-backed minority government. Lieberman has nevertheless said his party will recommend Eisenkot. Netanyahu is calling for a broad government under his leadership that excludes Arab parties, which he accuses of supporting terrorism and rejecting Israel’s Jewish character. President Isaac Herzog is due to receive the certified results and begin party consultations on November 4, then choose a lawmaker by November 11 to try to form a government. The nominee has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. If coalition efforts fail, further parliamentary steps could lead to a new election.
